opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, that was a very humbling period for me. Back when I was a student, restricted Boltzmann machines and deep belief networks were the exciting thing. Unsupervised pre-training felt like the path to deep learning, and I spent a lot of time trying to make those models work on larger image datasets, including ImageNet-scale data.

Honestly, it didn't work very well. I spent months tuning sampling procedures and learning rates and trying all kinds of tricks, and the results were never quite there. Then, around 2012, AlexNet came out: a convolutional network trained end to end with plain supervised learning on GPUs. It just blew everything away. That was a strange moment for me, because I realized the direction I'd been pushing on wasn't the one that mattered.

A few lessons stuck with me.

First, don't fall in love with a method. I was attached to RBMs because they were elegant. There's a nice probabilistic story and a beautiful energy-based formulation. But elegance doesn't guarantee progress. You have to stay honest about whether the approach is actually moving the needle on the problem you care about.

Second, scale and engineering matter much more than I appreciated at the time. Part of what made AlexNet win was the model design, but a big part was making the computation work: using GPUs, writing efficient kernels, getting enough data through the system. That realization pushed me toward systems. I started thinking that if I could build tools that let people run bigger experiments faster, that might have more impact than inventing yet another clever model. In a way, that thread runs through XGBoost, MXNet, and TVM.

Third, pick problems where you can get a fast, real signal. With RBMs on big data, the feedback loop was slow and murky. You'd wait a long time and still not be sure whether things were improving. Now I try to choose problems where I can see quickly whether something works, and where real users will tell me if it's useful.

So it was a "failure" in the narrow sense, but it shaped how I think about research. Be humble about your favorite ideas, take engineering seriously, and keep checking whether you're solving the problem or just enjoying the method.

r002.rationale: It discusses RBMs and ImageNet, but does not mention the KDD problem or favoring matrix factorization over RBMs.

r003.rationale: It describes moving away from RBMs, but does not say that sticking to one method would have prevented the team’s KDD results.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, that project was my first real lesson in what I'd call the economics of research. This was around 2011, 2012, when I was an undergrad at Shanghai Jiao Tong. Deep learning was just starting to look promising again, and restricted Boltzmann machines and deep belief nets were the hot thing. So I thought, okay, let me take this method everyone's excited about and push it to the hardest dataset I can find. ImageNet.

I spent almost a year on it. I built a GPU implementation of RBMs from scratch, I did all the engineering, I got it to actually run at that scale. And the result was... it worked, in the sense that it trained. But it didn't win. Then AlexNet came out, and the convolutional approach with supervised training just crushed everything. So in some sense the whole direction I had bet on was the wrong one.

But I learned two things from that. The first is that you have to be honest about why you picked a method. I picked RBMs partly because they were elegant and partly because they were fashionable, not because I had a strong argument for why they should win on that problem. The people who won had a clearer reason. Convolutions matched the structure of images. The supervised signal was abundant. The method fit the problem. So now when I choose a problem, I ask whether there's an actual structural reason the approach should work, or whether I just like it.

The second thing is more positive. Even though the research direction failed, the engineering didn't. All that time I spent making things run efficiently on GPUs, thinking about memory, thinking about how to make an algorithm actually scale, that became the real asset. It's basically what led into XGBoost, into MXNet, into TVM. So I came away believing that if you pick problems where even the failure mode leaves you with something durable, usually the systems and the tools, then you're never really wasting your time. The idea might be wrong, but the capability you build is portable.

So I tell students, choose problems where you can be wrong and still learn something you can carry with you.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention KDD, examining its problem, or choosing matrix factorization over restricted Boltzmann machines.

r003.rationale: The response does not discuss sticking to a single method or say that doing so would have prevented Chen’s team’s KDD results.

astra-6.text:
It taught me to be more problem-driven rather than method-driven. When you learn a technique like restricted Boltzmann machines, it’s tempting to ask, “Where can I apply this?” But applying a method to a challenging dataset doesn’t necessarily mean you’re addressing the right bottleneck.

The better starting point is: What problem do I want to solve, and why is this method a good fit? You can still have intuition and enthusiasm for an approach, but you need to be willing to change it when the evidence points elsewhere. That experience helped me separate attachment to a particular technique from commitment to solving the problem.

sol-6.1.text:
It taught me to separate the problem I cared about from the method I was excited about. You can spend a lot of time trying to make a particular model work, but the more useful question is: what is actually holding back progress on this problem, and is this method the right way to address it?

That doesn’t mean a difficult experiment is wasted. You learn from building things and seeing where they fail. But you have to be willing to change direction. I try to start with a meaningful problem, get feedback from experiments early, and let that evidence guide the choice of tools rather than becoming too attached to one approach.
